latin.300: Si quod enim foedus cum homine contrahit, id facit hominis causa, & quia bonum est homini. Hoc vero foedus, cuius ea est, quam Vir Doctus declarat, conditio, non poterat non esse Adami posteris damnosum. Multo plus enim ex eo erat metuendum mali, quam sperandum boni: nam ut inde ad nos aliqua utilitas rediret, opus erat ut Adamus toto vitae curriculo perseveraret in obedientia & fide erga Deum: nec tamen propterea, si Viro Docto fides habetur, nobis eius imputata fuisset obedientia, tantum qualis fuisset, tales nos genuisset: at, si vel semel ab obedientia deflecteret, prima eius inobedientia nobis omnibus imputanda erat ad mortis aeternae reatum, nec id tantum, sed ut ob imputatum illud peccatum puniremur infligenda nobis erat corruptio illa hereditaria quae vere peccatum est, & fons peccatorum. Qui factum est, ut Deus, qui ipsa bonitas est, & genus humanum amabat, aequiorem ei non tulerit conditionem, & qui Adamus non rogavit Deum, quandoquidem contrahebat cum Deo ut totius generis humani procurator, ut ab eo conditionem impetraret tolerabiliorem? Nam certe talis conditio ab odio potius quam ab amore profecta videri possit; nec quid ad Dei gloriam, ut omnia quae facit Deus, per se se conferre possit ullo modo intelligitur.
latin.301: Adde quod ea ratione aliter ad Adamum pertinuisset mandatum, aliter comminatio: illud ut ad caput generis humani, haec ut ad privatam personam: & vice versa ad nos pertinuisset comminatio, non item mandatum. Denique cur non ea conditione contractum est istud foedus, ut quemadmodum peccaret, sic etiam puniretur ut caput generis humani? Si recurras ad voluntatem Dei, quid opus erat ad has quaestiones alia responsione, quam generali ista, quia Deus ita voluit? Sed vide ne ei voluntatem attribuas pro tuo ingenio eius virtutibus minime convenientem, ac praeter Scripturam.
latin.302: GAR. Quaeritur secundo, Cur potius Adami peccatum posteris, quam posterorum Adamo imputatur? Resp. 1. Hoc inde esse, quod posteri omnes in Adamo radicaliter & seminaliter fuerunt. Adamus in posteris hoc modo non fuit. 2. Quod peccatum imputari, est poenam propter peccatum irrogari. Atqui poena peccatum ordine naturae semper insequitur, nunquam antecedit. Non potuit igitur Adamus poenas dare peccatorum, quae nondum erant, praesertim cum non ipse, sed Christus peccata hominum portare debuerit, & portando expiare.
latin.303: PLAC. Hac interrogatione non oppugnavi immediate imputationem immediatam primi peccati, sed rationem qua firmabatur, ideo scilicet primum illud Adami peccatum omnibus eius posteris imputari, quoniam Adamus componebat cum suis posteris unum corpus, cuius ipse caput erat, nos omnes eius posteri membra, quod autem facit caput toti corpori imputatur: objiciebam, si valet haec ratio, causam non esse, cur non itidem quae faciunt membra capiti, aut etiam toti corpori imputentur, quia reciproca est capitis & membrorum relatio. Itaque non attendens ad mentem meam, & loci, unde hanc interrogationem deprompsit, circumstantiam, Vir Doctus non ad rem respondet. Nam ad primam eius responsionem quod spectat, primo non est de ratione capitis ut sint in eo membra radicaliter & seminaliter. Deinde si de propagatione ageretur naturali, optima quidem esset ratio, cur propagatum fuerit peccatum ab Adamo in posteros, potius quam a posteris in Adamum, quia nempe posteri sunt ab Adamo, non Adamus a posteris: sed cum agatur de imputatione immediata, quae sit libera Dei actio, si spectavit posteros Adami tanquam eius membra unum cum eo corpus componentes, cur non potuit Deus aeque posterorum Adamo, atque Adami posteris peccatum imputare, praesertim cum posteri nullo modo causa fuerint peccati Adami, Adamus vero causa fuerit peccati posterorum?
latin.304: Ad alteram autem eius responsionem quod attinet, primum vivente Adamo eius filii & nepotes peccaverunt. Deinde ultimi diei judicium quae sequetur poena posterior erit peccatis posterorum Adami, & quidem omnium. Tertio cum imputatio sit actio Dei, & Deus tum habuerit praesentes omnes Adami posteros, habuit etiam praesentia eorum peccata, cur ergo ea imputare non potuit? Denique, si poena peccatum ordine naturae semper insequitur, nunquam antecedit, certe etiam peccatum ordine naturae semper insequitur existentiam eius cui imputatur, nunquam antecedit. GAR. Quaeritur tertio. Cum Adamus post peccatum illud primum continuo non desierit esse caput generis humani, cur non sequentia eius peccata aeque imputantur ac primum? Resp. 1. Quia unam unius offensam & inobedientiam, non plures memorat Apostolus, ob quam homines peccatores constituti fuerint. 2. Quia Adamus per primum illud peccatum suum, excussus est beneficio foederis illius, quod Deus cum toto genere in Adami persona pactus fuerat. Itaque etiamsi non desierit esse caput relatione originis, desiit tamen esse relatione foederis. Ad imputationem autem de qua loquimur, utrumque necessarium fuit, ut scilicet Adamus, & radix esset, unde genus humanum oriretur, & foederis depositarius, quod sibi & suis, aut conservaret, aut amitteret. Cum ergo posterior haec relatio capitis cessaverit per primum illud inobedientiae peccatum, nihil mirum si peccata Adami sequentia non imputentur, cum in eorum patratione priorem illam personam non amplius sustineret, neque caput esset eo modo, quo Deus ipsum initio constituerat.
latin.305: PLAC. Apostolus unam unius offensam & inobedientiam memorat, quia una illa offensa corrupit naturam unius, qualem autem iste unus habuit naturam, talem in suos posteros propagavit. Sed quid hoc ad imputationem antecedentem, quam Apostolus non docuit, & quae omnem propagationem naturalem antecedere putatur, & a Dei duntaxat voluntate pendere? Manet ratio, si ideo imputatur prima illa inobedientia, quia Adamus cum eam committeret nostrum erat caput, quando cum alias committebat nostrum etiam erat caput, debuerunt etiam aliae eius inobedientiae nobis imputari: eadem enim utrobique ratio est. Ad alteram responsionem, quam rursus a nescio quo foedere, cuius iam aliquoties meminerat, arcessit, dico illud foedus nec in sacris literis doceri, nec Deum decere, nec eius ullum fuisse beneficium, contra nos, non pro nobis constitutum: & quamvis eius beneficio, si quod erat, excussus fuisset Adamus, tamen remansisset vis obligandi ad obedientiam, & si minus ea praestaretur, ad augendam poenam. Alioqui quod fuit illud foedus? idem cum foedere quod vocant naturae, an ab eo diversum? Si idem, mansit obligatus Adamus ad obsequendum legi foederis naturae, eiusque omnia peccata foederis illius violationes fuerunt: cur ergo etiam illius foederis relatione caput generis non permansit? Si diversum, duo igitur cum Adamo, atque genere humano contracta sunt foedera, unum naturae, alterum quomodo appellabitur, (gratiae enim certe quidem non fuit) & cur huius violatio potius imputetur toti generi humano, quam illius, quod cum sit naturae, ad naturam hominum totam pertinet? Adde quod non intelligo, quare id foedus hominum caput constituerit Adamum, quod diu esse desiit, antequam Adamus quemquam gigneret? Nec quomodo Adamus dicatur caput generis humani relatione ad id foedus, sub quo eius posteri nunquam fuerant? Certe caput non fuit posterorum, si antequam ulli fuerint eius posteri, desiit esse eorum caput: nec opinor, dicitur caput relatione foederis, sed potius relatione ad posteros fundata in generatione. Ita non fuisset caput, nisi quo momento peccavit, hoc est, non fuisset caput nisi quando ii nondum fuerunt quorum diceretur caput, quando fuerunt non fuisset amplius eorum caput, quod concoquat qui potest, ego certe concoquere non possum.

pass_a.300: Placeus presses the invented covenant-condition: if God contracts with man, He does it for man's good—yet this foedus as the Learned Man states it could not but harm Adam's posterity. Far more evil was to be feared than good hoped. Lifelong obedience and faith still would not have imputed Adam's righteousness to us (only like begetting like); one single turn from obedience would charge us all with eternal-death guilt, and beyond that inflict hereditary corruption—true sin and the fountain of sins—as punishment for the imputed deed. How then did God, goodness itself who loved the race, not offer a fairer condition? And why did Adam, contracting as procurator of the whole human race, not ask God for a more tolerable term? Such a condition looks sprung from hatred rather than love, and it is hard to see how it of itself serves God's glory.
pass_a.301: Add the asymmetry: on that scheme the command would belong to Adam as race-head while the threat belonged to him as a private person—and for us the threat would reach us without the command. Why was the covenant not struck so that as he sinned he was also punished as head of the race? If you fall back on the divine will, every knot gets the same general answer—because God so willed. But take care not to ascribe to Him a will cut to your own ingenuity, least fitting His virtues, and beyond Scripture.
pass_a.302: Second erotema from GAR: why charge Adam's fall to the line rather than the line's sins back onto Adam? He answers first by radical and seminal presence of all posterity in Adam—not the reverse. He answers second by defining imputation as laying on a penalty: in nature's order penalty trails sin and never runs ahead, so Adam could not suffer for deeds not yet there; bearing and expiating human sin belongs to Christ.
pass_a.303: Placeus says the target was not immediate first-sin charging as such, but the body-prop used for it. GAR had treated Adam-plus-posterity as one body with Adam for head and us for members, so the head's act lands on the whole. Placeus's counter: if that logic stands, members' acts should land on the head the same way, because head and members trade relations both directions. The Learned Man skips Placeus's intent and the surrounding locus and so misses the mark. Radical-seed presence does not define what a head is. One-way natural begetting would explain corruption flowing Adam→posterity; a free divine charge would not be forced into that one-way mold—God could as well put posterity's guilt on Adam as Adam's on them, and the causal arrow already runs Adam→posterity, not back.
pass_a.304: Against GAR's second reply Placeus adds four points: Adam's sons and grandsons already sinned while he lived; the last-day judgment and following penalty come after all posterity's sins; God then had present both posterity and their sins, so why could He not impute them; and if penalty never precedes sin in nature's order, sin never precedes the existence of the one charged. Third erotema: why not Adam's later sins as well as the first, since after the first he did not at once cease to be race-head? GAR answers two ways: the Apostle remembers one offense and disobedience of one man, not several, by which men were constituted sinners; and by that first sin Adam was shaken out of the benefit of the covenant God struck with the whole race in Adam's person—so even if he did not cease to be head by origin, he ceased by covenant. For the imputation in view both were needed: Adam as root of the race and as depositary of the covenant he might keep or lose for himself and his. Once that later headship relation ceased through the first disobedience, later sins need not be imputed, for in committing them he no longer sustained that former person nor was head as God first set him.
pass_a.305: Placeus: the Apostle's one offense of one man explains corrupted nature passed by generation into posterity—not an antecedent imputation the Apostle never taught, thought to precede all natural propagation and to hang on God's will alone. The reason remains: if the first disobedience is charged because Adam was our head when he committed it, then when he committed others he was still our head, and those too ought to have been charged—same reason both ways. The covenant GAR keeps fetching is neither taught in the sacred letters nor becoming to God, nor was any benefit of it set against us rather than for us; even if Adam were shaken out of it, the binding force to obey would remain, and shortfall would increase penalty. Was that foedus the same as nature's covenant or different? If the same, he stayed bound to nature's law and all his sins violated it—why then did he not remain race-head by that relation too? If different, two covenants were struck, one of nature and another unnamed (certainly not of grace)—why impute violation of this rather than of nature's, which belongs to all human nature? Worse: how did a covenant that long ceased before Adam begot anyone constitute him head of men, or head by relation to a foedus under which posterity never stood? He was not head of posterity if he ceased before any existed; headship is founded in generation, not that foedus. So he would be head only at the sin-moment when they did not yet exist, and when they existed he would no longer be their head. Let who can digest that; Placeus cannot.

300: For if He contracts any covenant with man, He does it for man's sake, and because it is good for man. But this covenant, whose condition is what the Learned Man declares, could not but be harmful to Adam's posterity. For far more evil was to be feared from it than good hoped for: since for any utility to return from it to us, Adam had to persevere through the whole course of life in obedience and faith toward God; and yet even then, if the Learned Man is believed, his obedience would not have been imputed to us—he would only have begotten us such as he was; but if he once turned aside from obedience, his first disobedience was to be imputed to us all unto the guilt of eternal death, and not that only, but that we might be punished for that imputed sin there was to be inflicted on us that hereditary corruption which is truly sin, and the fountain of sins. How came it that God, who is goodness itself and loved the human race, did not offer it a fairer condition, and that Adam did not ask God—seeing he was contracting with God as procurator of the whole human race—to obtain from Him a more tolerable condition? For surely such a condition might seem to have sprung from hatred rather than love; nor is it in any way understood how it could of itself contribute to God's glory, as all things God does ought.
301: Add that on that account the command would have belonged to Adam one way, the threat another: the former as to the head of the human race, the latter as to a private person; and conversely the threat would have belonged to us, not likewise the command. Finally, why was that covenant not contracted on this condition, that as he sinned, so also he should be punished as head of the human race? If you fall back on the will of God, what need was there of any other answer to these questions than that general one, because God so willed? But see that you do not ascribe to Him a will suited to your own ingenuity, least fitting to His virtues, and beyond Scripture.
302: GAR. It is asked second: Why is Adam's sin rather imputed to posterity than posterity's to Adam? Reply 1. This is because all posterity were in Adam radically and seminarily. Adam was not in posterity in this way. 2. That to impute sin is to inflict penalty on account of sin. But penalty always follows sin in the order of nature, never precedes it. Therefore Adam could not pay penalties for sins that did not yet exist, especially since not he, but Christ, ought to bear the sins of men, and by bearing to expiate them.
303: PLAC. By this interrogation I did not immediately attack the immediate imputation of the first sin, but the reason by which it was fortified—namely that that first sin of Adam is imputed to all his posterity because Adam composed with his posterity one body of which he was head, we all his posterity members, and what the head does is imputed to the whole body: I objected that if this reason holds, there is no cause why what the members do should not likewise be imputed to the head, or even to the whole body, because the relation of head and members is reciprocal. And so, not attending to my mind, and to the circumstance of the place whence he drew this interrogation, the Learned Man does not answer to the point. For as to his first reply: first, it is not of the nature of a head that members be in it radically and seminarily. Next, if the question were of natural propagation, it would indeed be an excellent reason why sin was propagated from Adam into posterity rather than from posterity into Adam, because posterity are from Adam, not Adam from posterity; but when the matter is immediate imputation, which is a free act of God, if He regarded Adam's posterity as his members composing one body with him, why could God not equally impute posterity's sin to Adam and Adam's to posterity—especially since posterity were in no way the cause of Adam's sin, but Adam was the cause of posterity's sin?
304: As for his other reply: first, while Adam lived his sons and grandsons sinned. Next, the judgment of the last day, and the penalty that will follow, will be later than the sins of Adam's posterity, and indeed of all of them. Third, since imputation is an act of God, and God then had present all Adam's posterity, He also had present their sins—why then could He not impute them? Finally, if penalty always follows sin in the order of nature and never precedes it, surely also sin in the order of nature always follows the existence of him to whom it is imputed, and never precedes it. GAR. It is asked third. Since Adam after that first sin did not at once cease to be head of the human race, why are his following sins not equally imputed as the first? Reply 1. Because the Apostle mentions one offense and disobedience of one man, not several, on account of which men were constituted sinners. 2. Because by that first sin of his Adam was shaken out of the benefit of that covenant which God had struck with the whole race in Adam's person. And so even if he did not cease to be head by relation of origin, he did cease by relation of covenant. For the imputation of which we speak, both were necessary: that Adam be both the root whence the human race should arise, and depositary of the covenant which he might keep or lose for himself and his. When therefore this later relation of head ceased through that first sin of disobedience, it is no wonder if Adam's following sins are not imputed, since in committing them he no longer sustained that former person, nor was head in the way God had at first constituted him.
305: PLAC. The Apostle mentions one offense and disobedience of one man because that one offense corrupted the nature of one man, and such nature as that one had, such he propagated into his posterity. But what is this to an antecedent imputation which the Apostle did not teach, and which is thought to precede all natural propagation and to hang on God's will alone? The reason remains: if that first disobedience is imputed because when Adam committed it he was our head, then when he committed others he was also our head, and his other disobediences ought to have been imputed to us—for the reason is the same on both sides. To the other reply, which he again fetches from I know not what covenant he had already mentioned several times, I say that covenant is neither taught in the sacred letters, nor becoming to God, nor was any benefit of it constituted against us rather than for us; and even if Adam had been shaken out of its benefit, if it was any, there would still have remained the binding force to obedience, and if it were less performed, to increasing the penalty. Otherwise what was that covenant? The same as the covenant they call of nature, or different from it? If the same, Adam remained bound to obey the law of the covenant of nature, and all his sins were violations of that covenant: why then did he not also remain head of the race by relation of that covenant? If different, then two covenants were contracted with Adam and the human race, one of nature, the other—how shall it be named (for it was certainly not of grace)—and why is violation of this rather imputed to the whole human race than of that which, being of nature, belongs to the whole nature of men? Add that I do not understand why that covenant constituted Adam head of men which long ceased to be before Adam begot anyone; nor how Adam is called head of the human race by relation to that covenant under which his posterity never were. Surely he was not head of posterity if, before any of his posterity existed, he ceased to be their head; nor, I think, is he called head by relation of covenant, but rather by relation to posterity founded in generation. So he would not have been head except at the moment he sinned—that is, he would not have been head except when they did not yet exist of whom he would be called head, and when they existed he would no longer have been their head: let him digest that who can; I certainly cannot digest it.
